Back in May, I was selected for Jane Street's fully funded FOCUS program at their New York City headquarters, and this week's news brought one moment from it right back to mind. Watching Leopold Aschenbrenner's hedge fund go from $45 billion to a forced $16 billion fire sale to Citadel, after leverage and margin calls caught up with him, reminded me of my own screwup, a lot smaller and a lot less expensive. At FOCUS, we played a game called Estimathon, where teams race to answer estimation questions with no calculators, just gut instinct and reasoning under pressure. I guessed 100 billion for how many times a Taylor Swift song had been streamed. Not even close. Worse, I was so locked into figuring out NVIDIA's price on a specific day that I almost didn't realize the question was actually asking about trading volume. No money was on the line for me, obviously. But the same gap that made me blow those questions is the one that just forced a 4x leveraged portfolio into a fire sale. Being fast and confident isn't the same as being right, and that gap is exactly where risk lives, big or small. Beyond Estimathon, FOCUS gave me real time with people across trading, engineering, and strategy, plus office hours and networking that gave me a much clearer picture of what this world actually looks like day to day. Big thank you to Katie Nasta for putting the program together and being so generous with her time answering all our questions. Still have the cards they handed out, a good souvenir from a great few days. #quant

In the Bay Area, AI adoption is assumed. On the Eastern European border, it’s a reality check. Week 1 of Baltic AI Defense is officially in the books. Here is what we got done: • Deployed the MVP of a geospatial drone-detection system • Identified high-vulnerability blind spots along the eastern Latvian border • Prepped V2 and V3 - integrating deeper terrain data and optimizing our pathfinding algorithms. Two macro takeaways from the week: 1) The Baltics are unmatched. As someone who is half-Latvian, checking off all three Baltic countries this week was a personal milestone. Tallinn is easily a top-10 European city, and wrapping up the week on the beach in Klaipėda isn't a bad way to recharge. 2) The Silicon Valley bubble is very real. Outside of the Bay Area, the general understanding of AI’s actual utility is far more limited than we realize. Speaking with government officials in Estonia on Friday, it became clear that despite being a pioneer in digital governance, they face massive bottlenecks in deploying AI for defense - often defaulting to traditional EW like jammers over machine learning solutions. This left me with one recurring thought: Having the mandate and having the tools are two different things. Onto Week 2.

For my CS153 final project I built FARM, and in two months I'm bringing it to a factory in Dongguan, China to automate linework. For this generation of VLA models to hit reliable repeatability on multi-object tasks, you need a per-task prior, but fine-tuning a full policy per task is infeasible on compute and time, especially in low-volume factories where tasks change regularly. FARM runs on a full fine-tune of π.5, a GSE expert fine-tune, then a per-task LoRA. The LoRAs hotswap locally and are trained on ~30 demos each. They're 1% the size of the model, initialize per action in under 40ms, and cut mean joint error on held-out episodes by ~37%. On tasks already in the FFT-GSE training data, the LoRA layer can half joint error. Because they live locally on the floor, they compose into new skills over time. Give it a plain prompt and it will understand its surroundings and automatically choose appropriate LoRAs (skills) to achieve the task, working out what order to run them in and checking its work after each action. This planning step only needs to happen once and can be saved so the same line can run for weeks without continual LLM inference.
